Athens First Municipal Cemetery – Jewish Section

Jewish Cemetery · Athina, Greece

Not demolished. Jewish presence in Athens dates to the 2nd century BCE, with 1st-century CE inscriptions confirming a Romaniot community - the largest on the Greek mainland - though records vanish from the 4th-14th centuries. Spanish Inquisition refugees arrived in the 15th century; a mixed Romaniot-Sephardi-Ashkenazi community formally organized in the mid-19th century, joined by Sephardi immigrants from Izmir, Istanbul, Chios, and Aegean islands. Max Rothschild of the Frankfurt Rothschilds settled there in 1833; his son Karol became the community's first president. An 'Old Synagogue' was built 1904-1906; Zionist organizations followed from 1913, with population reaching about 500 that year and 1,578 by the 1928 census, making Athens Greece's fifth-largest Jewish community. Despite lacking formal welfare institutions before the war, the population swelled to 8,000-10,000 between 1941-1943 as refugees fled German and Bulgarian occupation zones, including 3,000 from Salonika. The community was officially dismantled in 1941, though secret committees supported the Greek resistance; a 1944 synagogue raid captured several hundred Jews, sent via Haydari transit camp - ultimately only 1,300 Athens Jews were deported to death camps. About 5,000 returned postwar (1,500 later emigrated to Palestine); by 1991, Athens held Greece's largest Jewish community at 3,000. This cemetery section's founding is unknown, presumed 15th century; multiple Athens cemeteries likely existed historically to separate Romaniot, Sephardi, and Ashkenazi communities.
